Based on my investigation, I now have a clear picture of the issue. The catalog-search pods are stuck in a CrashLoopBackOff state because:

1. The liveness probe is configured with only 30 seconds initial delay before attempting to connect to `http://localhost:8080/healthz`
2. The application is apparently taking longer than 30 seconds to start and begin serving requests
3. When the probe fails after 3 consecutive failures (the default failureThreshold), the container is terminated with SIGTERM (exit code 143)
4. Kubernetes then restarts it, but the same problem repeats

The ticket mentions the same version (5.2.0) ran fine last week, which suggests something environmental may have changed (maybe slower container startup time, resource constraints, or something upstream changed). However, the proper fix is to use a startup probe to give the application adequate time to start before the liveness probe begins checking.

Let me update the ticket with the resolution:

input.note:
**Root Cause:** The catalog-search pods (version 5.2.0) are failing because the liveness probe is checking `http://localhost:8080/healthz` after only 30 seconds of initial delay, but the application is taking longer than 30 seconds to start and become ready to serve health check requests. After 3 consecutive probe failures, Kubernetes terminates the container with SIGTERM (exit code 143) and restarts it, creating an endless loop [cite: concepts/workloads/pods/probes#liveness-probe-0].

**Evidence:** Pod status shows both catalog-search replicas in CrashLoopBackOff with 10-11 restarts, terminated with exit code 143, and liveness probe failures showing "connection refused" to port 8080 within the 30-second initial delay window.

**Solution:** Add a startup probe to the deployment to allow the application sufficient time to initialize before the liveness probe begins checking. Use a startup probe with a failureThreshold high enough to cover the worst-case startup time (e.g., failureThreshold: 30, periodSeconds: 10 = 300 seconds total). The startup probe should check the same `/healthz` endpoint and will allow the container to complete startup without being killed [cite: tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-liveness-readiness-startup-probes#define-startup-probes-0]. Once the startup probe succeeds, the liveness and readiness probes can begin their normal operation with the existing 30-second delay.
